content: Floris van Doorn created a new channel #Carleson.
This topic was moved here from #announce > new channels by Floris van Doorn.

I'm happy to launch the start of the Carleson project. This is a project aiming to formalize Carleson's theorem (Wikipedia) from a much more general version in so-called "doubling metric measure spaces". You are very welcome to contribute, no background in analysis required. For more info, head to the #Carleson stream.

Carleson's theorem is a notoriously hard result in analysis, with an inscrutable proof. Here is a recording to an introductory talk by me from last Monday about this project. However, the statement is deceptively simple. One version is that if you have a continuous periodic function f : ℝ → ℝ then the Fourier series of f converges pointwise to f almost everywhere (see the Wikipedia link for a more precise statement).

Along the way, we will also formalize a much more general version of Carleson's theorem. This version was proven by Christoph Thiele and his group last year. This proof has not been published yet (and has currently not even been submitted for publication). When discussion to collaborate on this project, Christoph Thiele and his group wrote an amazingly detailed blueprint for the proof, which can be accessed online here. This should make it possible for almost anyone to contribute that knows some Lean. There are significant parts of the proof that has a strong combinatorial flavor (e.g. chapters 4 and 5). So please head over to the #Carleson stream and claim a task!

You are completely right, sorry about that. I have some issues with the hosting via Github pages. I changed the link to a page that does work (and contains further links to the other parts of the project). EDIT: This is now fixed, thanks to Henrik Böving!

This announcement comes late, but a bit more than a month ago we fully finished the Carleson project.
We have updated the blueprint on arXiv with all major formalization authors, and we have submitted the regular mathematical paper for review, that now includes the remark that it has been fully formalized. That paper is also on arXiv.

I would like to (belatedly) thank everyone that has contributed to the project, and for the Lean and Mathlib communities that make such projects possible!
